name: healthy-object
intent: Ensure that objects are always created in a valid state by separating the collection of compulsory properties from object creation, using a dedicated Essence object that validates parameters before instantiating the target object.
problem: Many classes have compulsory properties that must be valid before an instance can be considered usable. In distributed or component-based environments where clients creating instances are outside the designer's control, there is no way to guarantee that clients will supply valid properties or validate objects after creation. Allowing invalid objects to be created leads to runtime failures, corrupted data, and inconsistent state.
context: Component-based or distributed systems where object creation is initiated by clients outside the designer's control (CORBA, ActiveX, microservices). Persistent objects where validity must be guaranteed before being used as dictionary keys, database indices, or before persistence operations. Situations where properties must be immutable after creation but cannot be enforced through language syntax alone.
benefits: Objects are never created in an invalid state: the CreationTarget is only instantiated after the Essence has validated all compulsory properties.
Compulsory properties are guaranteed immutable after creation: set methods exist only on the Essence, not on the CreationTarget.
Constructor exceptions are avoided: validation happens before object creation, not during it.
Interface coherence is preserved: manipulation and validation methods belong to the same class (Essence), making the API easier to understand.
Flexible parameter specification: different permutations of parameters can be supported without cluttering the interface with multiple constructors.
Reusable Essence: a single Essence instance can create multiple target objects with shared property values.
Early validation feedback: clients can call validateParameters() during parameter specification for interactive feedback.
Builder pattern compatibility: the Essence can be extended to create multiple related objects instead of a single target.
tradeoffs: Additional class overhead: introducing an Essence class adds complexity and may confuse developers who must understand which class to use.
Dual validation responsibility: validation logic may need to exist in both Essence and CreationTarget for properties that can be changed after creation.
Circular dependency: the Essence and CreationTarget classes depend on each other, requiring careful implementation (friend classes in C++, package-private in Java).
Increased indirection: clients must go through the Essence to create objects, adding a layer of abstraction.
State management complexity: the Essence holds state temporarily and must be kept alive until creation, unlike simple constructor calls.

participants.responsibility: A temporary object that collects and validates compulsory properties before creating the target object. Provides setter methods for each compulsory property, a validateParameters() method for early feedback, and a createTarget() method that performs final validation and instantiates the CreationTarget.

The actual domain object being created. Its constructor is restricted (private or protected) and receives a reference to its creating Essence to retrieve validated property values. Should be in a valid state immediately after construction.

Code that creates an Essence, supplies compulsory properties via setter methods, optionally validates early via validateParameters(), and finally calls createTarget() to obtain a valid CreationTarget instance.

use_cases: Persistent domain objects: a Contract that requires both a Supplier and a Customer at creation, where these relationships cannot be changed afterward.
Distributed systems (CORBA/ActiveX): clients outside the designer's control must create valid objects without direct constructor access.
Database-indexed objects: objects used as keys in dictionaries or database indices must have valid compulsory properties before being stored.
Immutable-property objects: properties that must remain fixed after creation but cannot be enforced through language syntax alone.
Form-based object creation: interactive clients can validate parameters incrementally as form fields are completed.
Domain objects with business rule validation: complex validation logic that depends on multiple properties must complete before object creation.
Microservices with external clients: services that cannot trust external callers to provide valid object state.
Workflow state machines: objects representing workflow steps that must transition through valid states from creation.
DDD aggregates and aggregate roots: entities that must enforce invariants across a cluster of related objects at creation time, preventing the aggregate from ever entering an invalid state.
Hexagonal architecture input ports: external adapters (REST controllers, message consumers) validate incoming data before it enters the domain layer, ensuring the domain never sees invalid input.
Data import and ETL pipelines: bulk operations where records must be validated as a batch before any are persisted, avoiding partial state corruption.
Event-sourced aggregates: command handlers that validate a command against aggregate state before producing events, ensuring only valid state transitions are recorded.
Read models and projections: view/store entities built from event streams must be constructed fully before being made available to queries.

Protocol Buffers Java builders: generated build() refuses to instantiate a message until all required fields are set, throwing UninitializedMessageException (with getMissingFields()) unless the caller explicitly opts out via buildPartial(); isInitialized() provides early feedback like Essence.validateParameters().

Java Immutables (@Value.Immutable): the generated builder tracks mandatory attributes and throws IllegalStateException naming the missing ones at build(), so immutable value instances are always constructed complete and consistent.

Compile-time essence enforcement: Immutables stagedBuilder (Style(stagedBuilder = true)) and staged/step builders return a new intermediate type after each setter so that build() only becomes reachable once every mandatory attribute has been supplied, making invalid creation sequences a compile error.
avoid_when: All object properties are optional: if there are no compulsory properties, the pattern adds unnecessary indirection.
Simple value objects: lightweight objects that can be fully constructed in a single constructor call.
Trusted, co-located clients: when all callers are under direct design control and can be relied upon to use constructors correctly.
Languages with named/labeled parameters: modern languages that support named parameters reduce the need for this pattern to handle cumbersome constructor lists.
Runtime reflection-based creation: situations where objects are created via dependency injection containers or ORM frameworks that manage validity separately.
anti_patterns: Anemic domain model: objects with no behavior, where logic lives in separate services, leading to objects that can exist in invalid states.
Constructor parameter bloat: forcing clients to supply dozens of parameters through constructors, making creation error-prone and APIs confusing.
Post-construction validation: allowing objects to be created in invalid states with separate validation steps that clients may skip.
Mutable compulsory properties: allowing compulsory properties to be changed after object creation, violating domain invariants.
Primitive obsession: using primitive types instead of typed value objects for compulsory properties, allowing semantically invalid combinations.
Partially initialized entities: repositories or factories that return entities with incomplete property sets for performance, breaking invariants and allowing impossible state transitions.
Specification pattern misused for new-object validation: requires instantiating an object in an invalid state first, violating Always-Valid principles.

Context-blind validation in constructors: embedding context-dependent validation (e.g., field required for web forms but not for data imports) in domain constructors makes the domain aware of presentation concerns.
design_principles: Encapsulation of creation: object creation details are hidden behind the Essence, preventing clients from bypassing validation.
Single responsibility: Essence handles parameter collection and validation; CreationTarget handles domain behavior.
Fail fast: validation happens before object creation, providing immediate feedback on invalid state.
Immutability of compulsory properties: once set on Essence and validated, compulsory properties cannot change in the CreationTarget.
Client safety: clients outside the designer's control cannot create invalid objects.
Declarative validation intent: use Assertion pattern to declare invariants where they are checked, not in comments.
Always-valid domain model: domain objects should never exist in an invalid state; construction is the first moment of their lifetime and must produce a valid instance.
Fail-fast at creation: invariant violations detected during construction should throw exceptions immediately, not return error codes that the caller might ignore.

Input validation vs invariant enforcement duality: the same business rule manifests as input validation (application layer, graceful error) and as invariant check (domain layer, exception); both must stay in sync.
best_practices: Distinguish compulsory from optional properties early in design: compulsory properties require Essence handling; optional ones can use standard setters.
Make CreationTarget constructors private or protected: prevent direct instantiation that bypasses Essence validation.
Keep Essence creation unrestricted: clients must be able to create an empty Essence to begin parameter specification.
Implement fluent setters on Essence: return self from setter methods to allow method chaining like essence.setCustomer(c).setSupplier(s).createTarget().
Provide validateParameters() for early feedback: allow clients to check validity at any point during parameter specification.
Place validation of immutable properties in Essence: validation for properties that cannot change after creation belongs in the Essence.
Place validation of mutable properties in CreationTarget: runtime validation belongs with the object that holds the property.
Use typed value objects instead of primitives: CustomerId instead of string, preventing semantic errors.
Consider using Essence as a Builder: extend Essence to create multiple related objects when needed.
Handle creation failure explicitly: return null, Null Object, or throw a specific exception rather than creating invalid objects.
Document the required creation protocol: clients must understand they must use Essence to create instances.
In C++, use friend classes to allow Essence access to private CreationTarget constructors.
In Java, place Essence and CreationTarget in the same package to allow package-private constructor access.
For distributed systems (CORBA), use Factory Objects as the source of Essence objects.

Apply the Always-Valid Domain Model principle: once a domain object is constructed it must be in a valid state. External input validation belongs at the application-service boundary (controllers, command handlers); domain constructors should throw exceptions on invariant violations.

Distinguish input validation from invariant enforcement: the same business rule appears as input validation (application layer, returns Result/error) and as invariant check (domain layer, throws exception). Both must be maintained together to avoid divergence.

Use Specification pattern only for existing objects: Specifications describe characteristics of already-existing domain objects. Do not instantiate an object just to validate it — this requires the object to enter an invalid state first.

Prefer strong typing over guard clauses for invariants: instead of if-checks that throw exceptions, use non-serializable types (e.g., a non-nullable EmailAddress wrapper) so invalid states are unrepresentable at the type level.

In hexagonal architecture, validate at the inbound adapter boundary: external callers (HTTP, messaging, CLI) should filter input before it reaches the application service. The domain model receives only data that already conforms to its invariants.

Gamma, Erich, Richard Helm, Ralph Johnson, and John Vlissides. Design Patterns: Elements of Reusable Object-Oriented Software (1994), Addison Wesley — Abstract Factory pattern.
Stroustrup, Bjarne. The Design and Evolution of C++ (1994), Addison Wesley — inspiration for the Essence pattern approach to named parameters.
Woolf, Bobby. Null Object. Pattern Languages of Program Design 3 (1997) — referenced in the Essence pattern paper.
Object Management Group. The Common Object Request Broker: Architecture and Specification (1995) — CORBA context for distributed object creation.
Cattell, R. & Barry, D. (eds). The Object Database Standard: ODMG 2.0 (1997) — ODMG database context for persistent object validation.

Palermo, Jeffrey. The Fallacy of the Always-Valid Entity. Programming with Palermo (2009) — https://jeffreypalermo.com/2009/05/13/the-fallacy-of-the-always-valid-entity/ — Critiques always-valid entity ideal; argues validation rules are context-dependent and error messages belong to the presentation layer.

Khorikov, Vladimir. Always-Valid Domain Model. Enterprise Craftsmanship (2021) — https://enterprisecraftsmanship.com/posts/always-valid-domain-model/ — Distinguishes input validation (application layer, Result) from invariant enforcement (domain layer, exceptions); hexagonal architecture view of boundary filtering.

Khorikov, Vladimir. Specification Pattern vs Always-Valid Domain Model. Enterprise Craftsmanship (2021) — https://enterprisecraftsmanship.com/posts/specification-pattern-always-valid-domain-model/ — Specifications should only validate already-existing objects; using them for new-object validation violates Always-Valid principle.

Khorikov, Vladimir. Partially Initialized Entities Anti-Pattern. Enterprise Craftsmanship (2016) — https://enterprisecraftsmanship.com/posts/partially-initialized-entities-anti-pattern/ — Repositories returning entities with incomplete properties break invariants; use DTOs for partial data and always return fully-initialized domain entities.

Klimenko, Alex. Builder Pattern Variations and Best Practices. Medium (2024) — https://medium.com/@alxkm/builder-pattern-variations-and-best-practices-643b6631341f — Covers fluent builder, nested builder, step builder; mandatory field handling and validation-before-build complementary to Essence pattern.

Carlson, Andy. Essence Pattern (full paper). PLoP 98 (1998) — https://hillside.net/plop/plop98/final_submissions/P10.pdf — Original 6-page paper: forces, solution structure, C++/Java/CORBA implementation, consequences, known uses (AT&T Rialto Repository).

Google. Protocol Buffers Java API: MessageLite.Builder and UninitializedMessageException — https://protobuf.dev/reference/java/api-docs/com/google/protobuf/MessageLite.Builder.html and https://protobuf.dev/reference/java/api-docs/com/google/protobuf/UninitializedMessageException — Real-world Essence: build() refuses to instantiate until all required fields are set; isInitialized() gives early validation feedback; buildPartial() is the explicit escape hatch.

Immutables project documentation — https://immutables.github.io/immutable.html and https://immutables.github.io/allstyles.html — Generated builders enforce mandatory attributes (IllegalStateException at build()); Style(stagedBuilder = true) and strictBuilder move compulsory-property enforcement to compile time.

Immutables issue #450: Calling final builder step without providing required arguments — https://github.com/immutables/immutables/issues/450 — Design discussion of staged builders as compile-time enforcement of mandatory attributes.

Buf. Protobuf Tip #8: Never use required — https://buf.build/blog/totw-8-never-use-required — Criticism of wire-level required fields; and protocolbuffers/protobuf issue #2497 — https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/issues/2497 — required was removed from proto3 because it breaks wire compatibility; enforce compulsoriness at the validation boundary instead.

Fowler, Derek. The Always-Valid Entity Anti-Pattern — https://blog.dezfowler.com/2009/05/always-valid-entity-anti-pattern.html — Criticism: constructor-enforced validity causes unreadable creation protocols, premature values, and exception-driven control flow; validate contextual rules outside the entity. See also Freestone, Jay. You might not need the always-valid entity — https://www.jayfreestone.com/writing/you-might-not-need-the-always-valid-entity/ — keep only core invariants in the object; contextual validity belongs to specifications/services.
